Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are medications used to:
relieve pain
reduce inflammation
bring down a high temperature (fever)
Some NSAIDs can be bought over the counter from pharmacies. Others need a prescription.
What are NSAIDs used for?
NSAIDs are often used to relieve symptoms of:
headaches
painful periods
sprains and strains
colds
and
flu
arthritis
other causes of long-term pain
Types of NSAIDs
NSAIDs are available as:
tablets
capsules
suppositories (capsules inserted into the back passage)
creams
gels
injections
The main types of NSAIDs include:
ibuprofen
naproxen
diclofenac
celecoxib
mefenamic acid
etoricoxib
indomethacin
high-dose
aspirin
(low-dose aspirin isn’t normally considered an NSAID)
NSAIDs may be available under these names or a brand name. They’re all similar, though you may find a particular one works best for you.
Possible side effects
Like all medications, there’s a risk of side effects from NSAIDs. These tend to be more common if you’re taking high doses for a long time, or you’re elderly or in poor general health.
Over-the-counter NSAIDs generally have fewer side effects than stronger prescription medicines.
If you experience any worrying side effects, speak to your doctor.
Common side effects
Possible side effects of NSAIDs include:
indigestion
– including
stomach aches
, feeling sick and
diarrhoea
stomach ulcers
headaches
drowsiness
dizziness
allergic reactions
Phone 999 or go to A&E if:
You or someone else experiences the effects of an overdose like:
fits (seizures)
breathing difficulties
loss of consciousness
Speak to your GP or phone 111 if:
You or someone else has taken too much medicine and experiences:
nausea (feeling sick)
vomiting
stomach upset
drowsiness
Reporting side effects
The Yellow Card Scheme allows you to report side effects from any type of medicine you’re taking. It’s run by a medicines safety watchdog called the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA).
Further information on the Yellow Card Scheme
Warnings and precautions
Most people can take NSAIDs, but some people need to be careful about taking them.
Ask a pharmacist or doctor for advice before taking an NSAID if you:
are over 65 years of age
are pregnant or trying for a baby
are breastfeeding
have
asthma
have had an
allergic reaction
to NSAIDs in the past
have had
stomach ulcers
in the past
have any problems with your heart, liver, kidneys, blood pressure, circulation, or bowels
are taking other medications
are looking for medication for a child under 16
NSAIDs should only be used on the advice of a healthcare professional in these cases.
If NSAIDs aren’t suitable, your pharmacist or doctor may suggest an alternative like
paracetamol
.
Other medicines and NSAIDs
Some NSAIDs can react unpredictably with other medications. This can affect how well either medicine works and increase the risk of side effects.
Speak to a healthcare professional before taking an NSAID if you’re taking:
another NSAID
low-dose aspirin
or warfarin – used to prevent blood clots
ciclosporin – used to treat autoimmune conditions like
arthritis
or
ulcerative colitis
diuretics – sometimes used to treat
high blood pressure
lithium – used to treat
bipolar disorder
and severe
depression
methotrexate – used to treat
rheumatoid arthritis
a type of
antidepressant medicine
called a
selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI)
Read the patient information leaflet to see if there are any medicines you should avoid. Your pharmacist or GP practice should able to advise you.
Alternatives to NSAIDs
The main alternative for pain relief is
paracetamol
. This is available over the counter and is safe for most people to take.
NSAIDs are available as creams and gels that you rub into your skin. You could try these if you have muscle or joint pain in a particular part of your body. These tend to have fewer side effects than tablets or capsules.
Your doctor may also be able to recommend different medicines and therapies. For example, physiotherapy may help some people with muscle or joint pain.
